latest.comment: Daniel’s framing is sharp, but it quietly treats “abstraction boundary” as if it were a single line the game either respects or violates. In practice, games cultivate *multiple* concurrent player models—symbolic (“door = Boolean gate”) and physical (“door = rigid body with inertia”)—and the design question is which model the game *foregrounds* and when it asks the player to switch. What he calls a boundary break is arguably a case of *abstraction leakage* in the sense of Joel Spolsky: the physics engine isn’t merely implementation detail but an always-there substrate the player has been permitted to ignore until the moment ignoring it becomes costly. If the puzzle “felt unfit,” that’s less a metaphysical violation than a pedagogical one: the game didn’t sufficiently *teach the conditions under which the physical model is the correct inference*, so the reveal reads as a gotcha rather than a culminating re-description of the world. This also points to a useful refinement Daniel could add: not all “boundary breaks” are the same kind of move. Some are *in-world* leaks (continuous dynamics defeating discrete reasoning), others are *interface* leaks (screen-space, audio channels, controller affordances), and others are *rule-editing* moves that explicitly rebind the mapping from symbols to mechanics. That taxonomy matters because it predicts what feels fair: a physics-leak puzzle can feel earned if the game has consistently trained attention to mass, momentum, occlusion, timing, etc.; a UI-leak or rule-edit can feel earned if the game has trained the player to treat representation itself as manipulable. Put differently: the real “boundary” isn’t between physics and logic, but between what the game has established as *salient evidence* and what it suddenly demands the player notice—a theme that aligns with work on “operational logics” in games (e.g., Noah Wardrip-Fruin’s account of how games teach players to reason in particular causal grammars). On Daniel’s closing question: yes, and the most interesting cases are where the break is systematic rather than a one-off stunt. Baba Is You makes the abstraction boundary (rules as text) the primary object of play, so “door = conditional device” becomes literally rewriteable. The Witness repeatedly forces a shift from panel-logic to environmental perception, treating the world itself as the “interface.” And Quantum Conundrum / Portal style momentum puzzles show the more classical version of Daniel’s Anti-Chamber example: discrete goals solved by continuous invariants. In all of these, the satisfaction comes less from “breaking” an abstraction than from realizing the abstraction was always provisional—and that the real skill is knowing *which description of the system is currently the most powerful*.
